summary: This informational RFC specifies scrypt, a password-based key derivation function that derives keys from a secret string. It relies on memory-hard functions, giving added protection against attackers using custom hardware. An ASN.1 schema is also provided.

plainLanguage.summary: scrypt derives keys from a password and salt using a computation that requires memory. RFC 7914 specifies the algorithm, parameter limits, encoding, and test vectors.

questions: what are scrypt n r p parameters
what do the scrypt parameters mean
subtitle: A password-based key derivation function designed to require memory

tldr.problem: Password-derived keys can be attacked by testing many possible passwords. Parallel custom hardware can reduce the cost of guessing when a derivation function uses little memory.
tldr.mechanism: scrypt applies PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256, a memory-intensive ROMix step built from BlockMix and Salsa20/8, and PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 again.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7914 specifies scrypt, its ASN.1 representation, and test vectors. It is informational and serves as a stable reference for the algorithm.

today: RFC 7914 is an Informational specification and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC describes itself as a stable reference for scrypt.

sections.title: Why scrypt Uses Memory
sections.content:
Password-based key derivation functions produce cryptographic keys from a secret value. Salts make precomputation more costly, and iteration counts slow each calculation. The RFC explains that parallel hardware can still lower the cost of brute-force password search.

scrypt is based on memory-hard functions intended to reduce the advantage of custom parallel circuits. RFC 7914 is a stable reference for scrypt; the document notes that the original scrypt paper predates it.
sections.plainLanguage: scrypt makes each password guess use memory as well as computation. This is intended to make parallel custom hardware less advantageous for guessing.

sections.title: Inputs and Tuning Parameters
sections.content:
scrypt takes a passphrase P, salt S, cost parameter N, block-size parameter r, parallelization parameter p, and desired output length dkLen. N must be greater than 1 and a power of 2. The RFC also sets upper bounds for N, p, and dkLen.

The user can tune N, r, and p for the available memory and computing capacity. At publication, the RFC says r=8 and p=1 appeared to give good results. A larger p can increase computational cost without increasing memory use.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameters control the work, memory, parallel processing, and output length. The RFC provides limits so implementations can reject unsupported values.

sections.title: How the scrypt Calculation Works
sections.content:
Salsa20/8 Core transforms a 64-octet input into a 64-octet output; the RFC notes that it is not a cryptographic hash function. scryptBlockMix applies this function to blocks and reorders the results. scryptROMix stores N intermediate values and then repeatedly selects and mixes stored values.

The complete scrypt algorithm uses PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-256 to initialize p blocks, applies scryptROMix to each block using N and r, and runs PBKDF2 again to produce dkLen octets. The memory table in ROMix is the step that requires substantial memory.
sections.plainLanguage: scrypt first expands the password and salt into blocks. It mixes each block with values stored in memory, then derives the requested key from the result.

sections.title: ASN.1 Representation and Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC defines an ASN.1 object identifier, id-scrypt, and a parameter sequence containing the salt, cost parameter, block size, parallelization parameter, and optional key length. The syntax is intended for use where PBKDF2 can be identified, including PKCS #8 and other key-management formats.

Sections 8 through 13 provide test vectors for Salsa20/8 Core, BlockMix, ROMix, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256, scrypt, and a PKCS #8 encrypted private key. Implementers can compare their outputs with these values.
sections.plainLanguage: The ASN.1 fields identify scrypt and its settings when another format stores a derived key. Test vectors give known outputs for checking an implementation.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Risks
sections.content:
The RFC notes that cryptographic algorithms may later be found weak. It describes ROMix as sequential memory-hard under the random oracle model, while scrypt's security depends on there being no shortcut for BlockMix with Salsa20/8 Core.

Passwords and intermediate values may remain in memory, core dumps, or swap after processing, so implementations should consider protected memory. Systems should also defend against denial of service from unreasonably large parameters. Poor settings that greatly reduce memory use can weaken the intended properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations need to protect passwords and intermediate values in memory. They must also prevent requests with extreme settings from consuming excessive resources.
